items.name: p07
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form geography and science YouTube documentary about the Mariana Trench and the deep sea. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices funny cartoon characters (a cheeky time-traveller, a cheerful little snailfish, a booming giant amphipod): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags. Pronounce place and scientific names clearly. VOICE IDENTITY (most important): the Narrator is always the same person: a low, warm baritone documentary host. Keep his voice identity and natural speaking pitch the same from the first line to the last, so it never sounds like a different or younger narrator. Emotion is welcome: show it freely through emphasis, energy, pace, louder and softer moments and dramatic pauses, as a real storyteller would. Never whisper or go breathy.
lines: Remember the Pacific Plate, sliding down under the Mariana Plate a few centimetres a year?
As the plate bends into the trench, it cracks. Seawater seeps into those cracks and soaks into the rock. And then that wet rock is carried down with the plate, deep into the Earth.
[horrified, looking at the sea] Wait. The ocean is... leaking?
In a way, yes. And in 2018, scientists found it's leaking much more than anyone thought.
A team from Washington University in St. Louis placed nineteen earthquake sensors on the floor around the trench and listened to the Earth shake for more than a year.
From those vibrations, they could tell how deep the wet rock goes. Their answer: almost thirty kilometres below the sea floor.

They estimated that around the Mariana Trench, about four times more water is being dragged into the Earth than earlier calculations said. And worldwide, through all these trenches, maybe three times more.
[checking his pocket watch, worried] So when does the ocean run out?
